subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Active Galactic Nuclei
description: A 60-second lesson on Active Galactic Nuclei.

hook.text: An active galactic nucleus, or AGN, is a galaxy center where the supermassive black hole is feeding and glowing.

buildup.text: Gas spirals into the black hole, forming an accretion disk that emits across the entire electromagnetic spectrum.

discovery.text: Carl Seyfert identified the first active galaxies in 1943. Their cores had unusually bright emission lines.

twist.text: Quasars, blazars, and Seyfert galaxies are all AGN—just viewed from different angles. Same engine, different view.

climax.text: The unified model says viewing angle determines what type we see. Face-on shows a quasar; edge-on shows a hidden nucleus.

punchline.text: Same monster, different angles. Perspective creates the zoo of active galaxies.

quiz.question: Why do quasars, blazars, and Seyfert galaxies look so different?
options: They are the same type of object viewed from different angles
They have fundamentally different types of black holes
They exist at different stages of galaxy evolution

details.summary: An active galactic nucleus (AGN) is a compact, extraordinarily luminous region at the center of a galaxy, powered by matter accreting onto a supermassive black hole.
details.whyItMatters: AGN reveal the most energetic steady-state processes in the universe. Their feedback regulates star formation in host galaxies, connecting black hole growth to galaxy evolution on cosmic scales.
takeaways: Ultra-luminous cores powered by supermassive black hole accretion
Can outshine the entire host galaxy
Unified model explains varieties through different viewing angles

faq.question: What is the unified model of AGN?
faq.answer: The unified model proposes that all AGN are fundamentally the same — a supermassive black hole with an accretion disk, surrounded by a dusty torus. Viewing angle determines what we see: face-on reveals the bright core (Type 1 Seyfert/quasar), edge-on hides it behind dust (Type 2), and looking down…

faq.question: Is the Milky Way's black hole an AGN?
faq.answer: Sagittarius A* is currently very quiet — it accretes very little matter and emits faintly compared to AGN. However, evidence suggests it was more active in the past (Fermi bubbles may be relics). If a large gas cloud fell in, it could temporarily become an active nucleus.
